power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = .83", Sentence = "Whether the option's gain is larger in harder tests depends on the measure and the specification: as declared (ω c without priors) it is, but in bits with priors mean proportion correct was not associated with the gain overall (p = .83), and in grade 8 the association went the other way."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. text.text: Right/wrong scoring of multiple-choice items discards information about which wrong option was chosen.
IRT models that use the choice date from 1972, but evidence on its value has come mostly in sample, one test at a time.

We compared option-level and right/wrong models on predicting the option chosen in held-out responses (log-loss, in bits) across 116 Item Response Warehouse tables (110 Brazilian), 469 TIMSS and PIRLS tests and 121 Czech exam forms.
In the warehouse, modeling the chosen option gained 15.4 millibits per response over the 2PL, 1.36 times the gain from estimating item discrimination.

Of the option's gain, 84% came from which wrong option was chosen, where right/wrong models use only distractor popularity; the rest, on whether the answer was right, was about a fifth of discrimination's gain.

The gain was positive in all 116 warehouse tables, in 119 of 121 Czech forms and, with priors on both models, in 463 of 469 TIMSS and PIRLS tests; relative to discrimination, it ranged from 0.8 (Czech exams) to 1.5 (ENEM).
By our declared measure, the gain peaked in the lowest ability deciles in most tables; per wrong answer, the choice improved prediction over distractor popularity most in the top decile.
The distractors are part of the item too (Thissen et al., 1989).

text.text: Operational scoring usually discards the choice: the response is coded 0 or 1 and modeled with a binary item response model, such as the one-, two-or three-parameter logistic model (1PL, 2PL, 3PL).
A review by Gierl et al. (2017) found comparatively little research on distractors.

text.text: This paper asks what the discarded information is worth.

We do not ask whether optionlevel models fit better in sample (with more parameters they usually will), but whether they predict the option chosen in responses they have not seen better than binary models do (Section 1.4).
Item response models that use the choice date from Bock (1972), whose nominal response model gives every option its own response function.
text.formatted: Item response models that use the choice date from <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Bock (1972)</ref>, whose nominal response model gives every option its own response function.

text.text: Bock reported that scoring all the options was substantially more precise than right/wrong scoring for test-takers below median ability and about as precise above it. Thissen (1976) found more information in the lower half of the scale when wrong responses to the Raven Progressive Matrices were modeled (as summarized by Haberman et al., 2019). Thissen and Steinberg (1984) added a latent "don't know" category whose responses spread over the options in estimated proportions, and Thissen et al. (1989) showed how such models serve item analysis. Suh and Bolt (2010) introduced the nested logit model: a 2PL, 3PL or four-parameter logistic model (4PL) for the correct response and, given an incorrect response, a nominal model among the distractors, a structure that Bolt et al. (2012) present as a natural way to evaluate what distractor selection adds to scoring.

text.text: What the wrong options of keyed multiple-choice items add to prediction, the question of this paper, was not part of that work.

This study compares option-level and right/wrong models out of sample with one design and the IRW's yardstick across many tests: 116 tables of the warehouse (110 of them Brazilian) and, as replications outside it, 469 Trends in International Mathematics and Science Study (TIMSS) and Progress in International Reading Literacy Study (PIRLS) tests and 121 forms of the Czech national exams.
It asks:  R1 (how much): How much does modeling the chosen option improve held-out prediction over binary models?
 R² (where): Where on the ability scale is that gain largest?
 R3 (choice and ability): How does the choice among wrong options relate to ability?
Because binary models predict which wrong option is chosen only from distractor popularity (Section 3.2), we answer R1 for the option chosen and for correctness alone.
We also compare the gain, in bits, with that from estimating item discrimination, as Haberman et al. (2019) did in sample (exploratory; Section 3.4).

text.text: We answer R3 with the spread of choices among wrong options by rest-score decile and with an external criterion for ability.
We then ask which model predicts best, whether the gain holds for test-takers unseen in calibration and how many test-takers are needed before it pays.
The assumption that random guessers spread evenly over the options is tested by a model comparison (Section 5).
The primary measures of R1 to R3 and some secondary analyses were planned before the main run; the rest were added afterwards and are exploratory (Section 3.10).

Estimating ability from wrong answers and correlating it with the full-test estimate, which contains those same answers, is circular.
In each of 3 samples per table, items were split at random into halves A and B and persons into five folds; models were calibrated on 80% of the persons.

text.text: For each held-out response, a model's log-loss is -log 2 of the probability it gave to the option actually chosen: 1 bit for a probability of 1/2, 2 bits for 1/4 and 0 for 1.
The gain of model b over model a is the drop in mean log-loss, in bits per response; we report millibits (thousandths of a bit).

The loss splits exactly into two parts (Appendix B): the loss on whether the response was correct, the only part on which binary models differ from one another (Section 3.2), and, for wrong responses, the loss on which wrong option was chosen.
Because the parts add up to the total, the gain from the option can be split into correctness and which wrong option, and compared with the gain from discrimination on one scale.

Our declared measure for R², ω c 2PL → nominal by decile of the 2PL ability estimate, was highest in the two lowest deciles in 92 of the 116 tables (ENEM 33 of 52, ENCCEJA 51 of 56, other tests 8 of 8) and in the two highest in the other 24; the decile of the maximum was higher in harder tables (Spearman -.68 with the mean proportion correct; ENEM -.72, ENCCEJA -.40).

text.text: Low scorers' choices are concentrated.
Among chance-level scorers (a median of 38% of persons per table), a favorite distractor drew a median of 35% of their wrong answers per item in ENEM (chance: 25%) and 47% in ENCCEJA (chance: 33%).
The choice became more concentrated as ability rose: the median share of the favorite distractor went from 34% to 47% in ENEM and from 46% to 57% in ENCCEJA.
This says that low scorers' choices are not uniform, not that low scorers do not guess; whether guessers spread evenly over the options is tested in Section 5.

Table 3 gives the median correlation of each scoring of half A with ability on half B. Scoring the option raised the correlation from .688 (2PL) to .721 (nominal) in ENEM and from .601 to .622 in ENCCEJA, and improved it in 115 of 116 tables.

The choice among wrong options alone, without knowing whether the person answered correctly, correlated .492 with the criterion in ENEM and .358 in ENCCEJA, against .033 and .045 with the letters shuffled; it exceeded its null in all 116 tables, and its partial correlation given the number correct (.27 and .22) was positive in all 116.
Against right/wrong 3PL scoring.
INEP scores ENEM with a 3PL and EAP (INEP, 2011, 2012).
Our 3PL uses the same model and estimator, but not INEP's item parameters or prior, and scores half a test; the comparison is therefore with right/wrong 3PL scoring, not with the official score.

In the full 2023 ENEM microdata (500,000 test-takers scored with item parameters calibrated on independent samples; criterion: the official score from the other test day), scoring the option (nested logit with guessing) instead of right/wrong (3PL) raised validity in all four areas and left socioeconomic and racial gaps per unit of validity unchanged (ratio 0.98 to 1.02 across 4 areas and 5 group contrasts).

text.text: Mostly Brazil.

Of the 116 warehouse tables, 110 are Brazilian, and the unit of replication is the program, not the table: outside Brazil the replication rests on TIMSS and PIRLS, which need priors at their sample sizes, and on two Czech exams, where the gain was smaller.
We make no claim about multiple-choice tests in general.

The threshold of about 1,000 responses per item between maximum likelihood and priors was chosen after looking at the results, from the sample-size curve, which places the crossing between 400 and 800 responses per item, and from TIMSS 2023 grade 8, with about 760.

The priors are not neutral: both sets center the distractor slopes where the nominal model reduces to the 2PL with fixed distractor shares, so they shrink toward the binary baseline, and the prior on the key slope also restricts its sign (Table A1); and the two prior sets in use below the threshold give different counts at N = 250 (Section 4.7).

text.text: The table-level SE comes from 10 samples that overlap by chance, so it understates the SE relative to the population; with the correction, ω c stays above two SE in the ENEM and ENCCEJA tables (Appendix B).
Folds are random over cells, and the halves A and B and S and T are random over items, so a held-out item can share a passage or stimulus with training items of the same person.
If the choice of distractor reflects how that person read the shared material, part of the option's gain could come from that dependence rather than from ability.
The concern is largest in PIRLS, where every item belongs to a passage; we did not run folds that keep a passage together.
Exploratory comparisons and populations.

The 3PL and nested-logit comparisons in the ability analysis are exploratory, our 3PL is not INEP's scoring, and our 3PL and 3PLNRM are at the posterior mode reached from mirt's solution, which need not be the only mode (Section 3.1).
New test-takers come from the same table and year as the calibration sample, so that task does not show that the gain generalizes to other populations.
The sample-size thresholds are readings of a curve in 20 tables, not tested cut-offs.
Group gaps.

The analysis of group gaps covers one exam and one year, and the data do not separate whether the tilt it finds reflects option-level differential functioning or model misfit where guessing is common.

On whether the answer is right, it was about a fifth of the gain from discrimination.
The size is not a constant: it depends on the calibration sample, and in the Czech exams it was about a third of Brazil's and below the gain from discrimination.

text.text: It also answers part of the concern that the information of option-level models is an artifact (García-Pérez, 2014): held-out responses confirm that some of it is real, and across tables the promised gain (the Fisher information ratio) and the collected gain (the correlation with the other half of the test) were ordered alike (Spearman .76).
Against the 3PL, the gain on correctness disappears overall and reverses in ENEM, and in ENEM mathematics the nominal model only ties with the 3PL as an ability estimator.

Both results are consistent with one mechanism: in ENEM, a large part of what the option adds at the bottom of the scale is structure that a guessing floor also captures (the 3PL itself gained 4.1 millibits over the 2PL there, more at later booklet positions; Section 4.1).

A model with both (the nested logit with guessing) predicted best in the Brazilian tables, also against the nominal model with priors, and tracked ability better than right/wrong 3PL scoring in 113 of 116 tables (Section 4.5).
The classical statement is that option scoring helps most below the median (Bock, 1972).

The comparison can be run on any table that keeps the chosen option, and its inputs are those of the warehouse's own yardstick: held-out cells, the IMV and ω c .

The analysis also produced an item-and option-level layer for the 116 tables (4,492 items and 20,385 options: option parameters, ω c per item and informative distractors), rebuilt with the nominal model at its maximum, to be released with the code upon publication.

For users, the model and its fit matter: mirt's default parametrization of the nominal model can stop short of the maximum (Appendix A), and where guessing is common, a model with both a guessing floor and the option predicted better than either alone.
These results quantify information; they do not by themselves argue for changing how any exam is scored.

Partchev (2020) held that high-stakes scoring rules should be fixed in advance, easy to explain and accepted as fair, and so advised investigating the information in wrong responses in research rather than exploiting it in assessment.
Two choices in this study call for a specification fixed in advance: a single prior for samples below about 1,000 responses per item, and folds that respect shared passages.
Kanopka and Domingue (2025) noted that their position-sensitive mixture used only a 1PL kernel, a limitation of that work.
A nominal kernel is one way to lift it.
Which wrong option a test-taker chooses carries information that right/wrong scoring discards.
Measured on responses the models had not seen, that information improved the prediction of the option chosen in every program we studied.

text.text: The fix.

With a1 fixed at 1 and all slopes free except that of the reference distractor, the model is the same (the map between the two sets of slopes is one to one when the key slope is not zero) and mirt reaches the maximum, with the same EM, the same quadrature, the same cap of 2,000 cycles and the same EAP.

In the 5,800 folds of the warehouse tables, all fits converged (a median of 63 cycles, at most 841), the training log-likelihood rose by a median of 17 units over the default fit (at most 277), and the 6 folds in which the default fit had degenerated without the convergence flag detecting it disappeared.
In 34 folds an independent optimizer checked the maximum.

In 11 folds of 11 tables, the refit came within 0.005 log-likelihood units of the maximum found by an independent EM (the default convergence tolerance of mirt), and the default parametrization started from the refitted solution stayed there and predicted the same (largest difference in the probability of the chosen option, 3.4e-4).
In 23 other folds of 22 tables, a quasi-Newton optimizer started from two points reached the same solution, between 0.0002 and 0.011 units above the refit.

Out of sample, the refitted model predicted better than the default fit in 104 of the 116 tables (100 by more than two SE; median gain 0.39 millibits per response) and worse in 12 (8 by more than two SE), all by 0.08 millibits or less.

With the priors of Table A1, the default parametrization reaches the posterior mode: in 12 folds of the TIMSS and PIRLS fits, five versions of the fit (an independent optimizer from two starting points, and mirt by default, with a tighter tolerance and from another start) gave the same log-posterior and the same held-out gain.

text.text: These fits stopped below the posterior maximum while reporting convergence (by 0.5 to 102 log-posterior units in 480 fits of 24 tables), and a tighter tolerance did not change this.
The cause is not that of the nominal model.

In mirt, up to the current release (1.48) and including the version we used, the log-density of the expbeta prior is correct but its first and second derivatives are taken with respect to g rather than its logit, the parameter the EM updates; the prior then pulls g toward its mode more strongly than intended, and the EM settles at a point that is not the posterior mode.
Xiao (2026) documented the error, which is corrected in the development version 1.48.2; we observed the stop independently.

We therefore polished every fit of the two models in the main analyses (5,800 fits of the 3PL, 3,200 of the 3PLNRM in the comparison of Section 4.3, 11,600 in the analysis against the other half [all 10 samples, for the standard errors of Section S10.2] and 3,480 for new test-takers) to the posterior mode reached from mirt's solution, maximizing mirt's log-posterior with the derivatives of the prior taken with respect to the logit of g, and the figures in the main text are at that mode.
The posterior can have more than one mode: from other starting points a higher one exists in some fits.
No sign changed, and the counts moved in favor of the 3PL and the 3PLNRM.
In 8 fits of the psychTools and vocabulary tables the maximum is at infinity, because a distractor was never chosen in the training data; the two counts that this moves are given both ways.

The other analyses that use these two models were polished in the same way: 40 fits in the group-gap analysis, 208 for the short form, 100 in the comparison with the mixture with uniform guessing, 3,025 nested logits in the Czech exams and 1,240 fits in 124 TIMSS and PIRLS tests (all 84 of TIMSS 2019 grade 8 and 10 at random from each other database).
In TIMSS and PIRLS, polishing moved the 3PLNRM against the nominal model (Section S8).
The chance-filter check (Section S10.5) and the per-database gaps between the 3PLNRM and the nominal model in Section S8 keep mirt's fits.

The guessing vignette cited in Section 1.3 fitted its 3PL in mirt with the same prior before the correction; it reports that, without any prior on g, the 2PL → 3PL gain stayed positive in the three tables where it checked this.

Results.

Scored with the 3PLNRM, the short form reached, with a median of 8.4 items, the correlation with the 2PL score on the held-out half that right/wrong 3PL scoring reached with 10 (.696 against .685 after 10 items); with the other test day as criterion, 8.9.

In a linear test with the full 45-item area and the other test day as criterion, nominal scoring matched 2PL scoring with 30% fewer items (median of 52 tests), in line with what Fisher information implies (28%), although not test by test (from about 10% in the human sciences to 41% in the natural sciences).

Table by table, the measured saving exceeded the one Fisher information implies in 26 tests and fell short in 23, and in 3 (all in human sciences) nominal scoring did not reach the correlation of the 2PL with the full area.
With a 22-item half as the test and the other half as criterion, the saving was 24%.

This 28% compares the nominal model with a separately fitted 2PL; the 38% of Section 4.4 of the main text compares the option's information with the correctness part of the same nominal model, and the two are different quantities.
With the letters of the distractors shuffled, there was no saving.
Data.

Three disjoint calibration samples of 20,000 test-takers and one scoring sample of 500,000 different test-takers.
Items: 45 in natural sciences, 45 in human sciences, 40 in languages (without the foreign-language items) and 43 in mathematics.
The criterion of each area is the mean official INEP score in the two areas taken on the other test day.
Group contrasts (focal against reference): school type, family income, mother's education, race, region and sex.

In each area and calibration sample we fitted the 3PL and the nested logit with guessing (3PLNRM) with mirt's EM under the priors of Table A1 of the main text (polished to the posterior mode reached from mirt's solution; Appendix A of the main text), and scored the 500,000 test-takers by EAP on a grid of 61 points from -4 to 4 with a standard normal prior.

For each area, contrast and score: the standardized gap d, the validity r (the correlation with the criterion) and d/r, the gap per unit of validity, which removes the attenuation that measurement error causes in both; the gap at equal criterion, γ, from a regression of the score on a restricted cubic spline of the criterion (5 knots) and the group, divided by r, with ordinary least squares weighting and with weighting by the focal group; and differential prediction in the sense of Cleary, from a regression of the criterion on a spline of the score and the group.
Option-level differential functioning is what the literature calls differential distractor functioning (Green et al., 1989; Penfield, 2008; Suh & Bolt, 2011).

text.text: Two simulations without option-level differential functioning that reproduce the observed validity serve as nulls: a generative one, in which ability is drawn from a latent regression on the criterion and the groups and all responses are simulated from the 3PLNRM (validity within -0.004 and +0.003 of the data), and a conditional one, which keeps each response's correctness and redraws only the distractor chosen.
A permutation of the group label within each contrast (20 times) gives the noise floor of the change in γ/r (standard deviation at most 0.0034).
Results.

Scoring the option raised validity in all four areas (natural sciences .694 to .733, mathematics .694 to .709, human sciences .738 to .741, languages .703 to .708, without the 3,547 test-takers who left a whole area blank).
The ratio of d/r under option scoring to d/r under right/wrong scoring was 0.98 to 1.02 across 4 areas and 5 group contrasts (sex is reported separately).
Raw gaps widened slightly, as expected from a more valid score (for example, the income gap in natural sciences went from 1.315 to 1.361 standard deviations of the score).

Against the simulations, the option did not shift disadvantaged groups uniformly: in 20 of 20 area-by-contrast cells it placed them higher among low scorers (the three lowest deciles of the criterion) and lower among high scorers (the three highest); the mean shift, within ±0.03 SD, changed sign with the weighting.

The 3PL overpredicted the disadvantaged group on the other day (in natural sciences, income: -0.371 SD of the criterion), and the 3PLNRM overpredicted it less in the 20 cells, which is what its higher precision predicts.
For sex, the option placed women higher at equal criterion in natural sciences (about 0.04 SD).
The data do not separate whether the tilt reflects option-level differential functioning or model misfit where guessing is common.

text.text: The figures without priors (354 of 469 tests; 0.93 times discrimination) are not maximum likelihood estimates: the EM was stopped at 2,000 cycles, and in part of the folds, including some flagged as converged, a slope grows without bound and the likelihood has no finite maximum; taken to the maximum, the gain fell in 8 of 9 tables checked and rose in one.

The priors are not neutral either: of the six tests in which the option did not pay with priors, in two (Côte d'Ivoire, grade 8 mathematics, and Morocco) the key-slope prior forces keys that the data place below the reference distractor, and in 7 tests the nominal model without priors predicted better than with them.

In two simulations from a fitted nominal model, the fit with priors recovered 31% and 42% of the gain of the true model and the fit without priors 6% to 7%, so the gains reported are probably conservative.
The share of the gain from which wrong option was chosen (70% to 78% by database) was below Brazil's under the same priors and sample size (81% to 93%).

The nested logit with guessing predicted right or wrong better than the 3PL, but in total log-loss it predicted worse than the nominal model with priors in all five databases (by 0.8 to 5.9 millibits per response with mirt's fits).

At the posterior mode the gap widened: in TIMSS 2019 grade 8, refitted in full, from 0.8 to 1.7 millibits (1.3 without the items whose maximum is at infinity in some fold), and in 10 random tests of each other database the median change was negative.
Unlike in Brazil, with about 600 responses per item and no prior on its distractor parameters, the mode overfits them.
Of the 463 tests with a positive gain with priors, 428 exceeded two fold-based SE, and 367 with that SE multiplied by 1.8, the factor by which one replication per table understates it in bits.

Against the replication criteria fixed beforehand, the result held in part: in TIMSS 2019 grade 4, 89% of the tests had a positive ω c , against the 90% required; the criterion on the ratio to discrimination was met only with priors; and the share from which wrong option stayed below the 75% required (51% without priors; 74.6% with priors, an exploratory reading).

Whether the option's gain is larger in harder tests depends on the measure and the specification: as declared (ω c without priors) it is, but in bits with priors mean proportion correct was not associated with the gain overall (p = .83), and in grade 8 the association went the other way.
High-performing countries gained less, but gained (12 of the 13 TIMSS 2019 grade 4 tests from countries scoring above 560 points).

Across the 469 tests, a meta-regression of the gain with priors on both models, in bits, on the number of responses per item, mean proportion correct, items per student, subject, grade, mode, script and the country's mean performance, with random effects of country, database and test, was read with decision rules fixed before it was run; one rule, for correlated moderators, was specified after a first look at the coefficients and changed no verdict.

The gain grew with the responses per item: +1.53 millibits per standard deviation [1.19, 1.87], about 2.3 per doubling, from +1.51 to +1.59 under other random-effects structures and with the SE multiplied by 1.8 or 2.
Within three tests, repeating the analysis with priors on two disjoint halves of the students lowered the gain by 2.3 to 4.7 millibits, which is what the size of the calibration sample predicts.
Test difficulty and country performance were too correlated (r = .83) to separate, and mean proportion correct alone had no association (+0.04 [-0.36, 0.44]).
The association with items per student is fragile: with the database as a fixed effect it was +0.51 [-0.08, 1.10].

With a1 fixed at 1, modeling the option reduced held-out log-loss in 119 of 121 forms, gained 0.80 times as much as discrimination and drew 77% of its gain from which wrong option was chosen, against 84% in Brazil with the same fit.

With the default fit, the count was the same (119 of 121), the gain was smaller than in Brazil with the same fit (5.6 vs 14.9 millibits per response, about a third; about half of Brazil's four-option ENCCEJA) and, pooled, smaller than the gain from item discrimination (ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.96): about as large in the Czech-language tests (1.17, 0.95 to 1.36) and about half as large in the foreign-language tests (0.54, 0.47 to 0.63), where discrimination adds much more.

In mirt 1.47, the default parametrization of the nominal model is P k ( θ )∝ exp( a1 ⋅ ak k ⋅ θ + d k ), with the slope multiplier of the reference category fixed at 0 and that of the last category at m -1.

In 60 of 60 folds of 12 warehouse tables, checked with an EM of our own (and, in one fold of 8 of them, also with TAM and with mirt itself with a1 fixed at 1), the EM stopped below the maximum while reporting convergence, a median of 24 log-likelihood units below it (at most 87).
The cause is the product a1 • ak: the EM enters a valley with a1 very small (0.001 to 0.07) and ak very large, and moves more slowly than the convergence tolerance.
This is the parametrization of Thissen et al. (2010), with an overall slope and category scoring values anchored at 0 and m -1.

text.text: The documentation of mirt warns of the symptom, though not of a stop below the maximum: the nominal model can become numerically unstable when poorly chosen high and low anchor values push ak above 10 in absolute value, and it recommends anchors that keep the estimates between 0 and m -1, chosen on theoretical grounds or by reestimating after convergence (Chalmers, 2026).

ENEM gives the same items in several booklets in different orders and hands the booklets out by seating position so that neighbors differ, which Kanopka and Domingue (2025) treat as random.

For each of the 52 ENEM tables, we linked every test-taker in the 10 samples to their booklet in INEP's public microdata (INEP, n.d.-b) and each item to its position in that booklet (1 to 45 within the area, with the foreign-language items of languages in positions 1 to 5); every held-out cell was matched, and in the natural sciences and mathematics cells of the first sample of each year the stored correctness agreed with the microdata in all cells.

With the fits of the main analysis and no refitting, we regressed each held-out gain on the item's position after removing each item's mean (one pooled within-item slope per sample) and averaged the slopes over the 10 samples (SE across samples, too small for the reason given in Appendix B of the main text).

The 2PL overpredicted correctness more the later an item appeared, by 0.9 percentage points per 10 positions on average (by more than two SE in 51 of 52 tables, also with the SE multiplied by the factor of Appendix B), a position effect in the sense of Kanopka and Domingue (2025).

The nominal model's standing against the 3PL on correctness fell with position in 51 of 52 tables (by more than two SE in 45, and in 43 with the factor).

In languages, which always opens its test day, the nominal model was not behind the 3PL in the first 15 positions in any of the 13 years; in mathematics, which always follows 45 items of another area on the same day, it was behind from its first 15 positions in all choice response records more than correctness.
